USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Go into the G20 Osaka meeting with Xi holding our current leverage but seeking a Buenos Aires-style truce: resume negotiations, keep existing tariffs and the Huawei entity list in place, and refrain from activating the threatened next $300B round absent real progress. Do not further escalate before or during the summit; use the meeting to restart the negotiating track and lock in a freeze on escalation, positioning any tariff concessions as conditional on China's structural commitments.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is moderately elevated, not existential. The real US economy is still strong (consumer sentiment 98.2, benign CPI, industrial production roughly flat per country_health), and Washington holds substantial leverage (25% tariffs on ~$250B already live since List 3 rose to 25% on 2019-05-10, plus the Huawei entity list added 2019-05-16). The threat drivers are forward-looking and political: the 10-yr Treasury yield has collapsed from ~2.69% (late 2018) to 2.05% by 2019-06-26 with the 2-yr at 1.77%, compressing the 10s-2s curve toward inversion — markets pricing growth/recession risk from the stalemate — and the farm belt is in acute pain (China, formerly buyer of ~1/3 of US soybeans, has stopped buying), forcing a second aid package ($16B announced May 23) and drawing public balking from GOP senators like Grassley ahead of 2020. Reuters' pre-summit reporting described a 'poisonous atmosphere' and low expectations, with the likeliest favorable path a temporary truce that postpones the $300B threat. Against that backdrop, further escalation is the wrong move: it would deepen market stress, intensify farm-belt/domestic political blowback, and alienate allies we need for WTO reform — while a negotiate/hold stance preserves all our bargaining chips and sets up a conditional de-escalation. Action is thus mild de-escalatory posture (negotiate, ~+0.1), not concession: no rollbacks or purchase commitments until China offers matching structural concessions.

Farm-belt political cost: second aid package ($16B, May 23); Grassley/GOP balking

Low pre-summit expectations; most likely outcome a truce postponing $300B round

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Go into the G20 Osaka summit (Xi-Trump meeting agreed June 18) seeking a truce that halts further US escalation — specifically to delay the threatened 25% tariffs on the remaining ~$300B of exports and to resume suspended talks. Do not raise the stakes or capitulate to structural demands (IP/forced technology transfer) that infringe sovereignty; hold the line, defend our position as the defender of rule-based trade, and signal readiness to resume equal consultations while keeping retaliation tools (rare-earth exports, unreliable-entity list) in reserve.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading is driven by hard, current evidence: US already applies 25% tariffs on ~$250B of our goods and placed Huawei on the Entity List (May 16), Google suspended Android/GMS and US chip suppliers paused sales (May 20) — the firm-level targeting called out in the CHN +0.5 anchor. The real economy is already biting: official manufacturing PMI fell to 49.4 in May (contraction), with new-export orders dropping to 46.5 and the employment sub-index at its lowest since March 2009, while the yuan has depreciated ~3% since the tensions flared and the IMF cut our 2019 growth forecast to 6.2% (weakest in 29 years). This is high but not existential pressure — GDP growth remains around 6.2%, reserves are ample, and Beijing is already rolling out stimulus. It does not warrant maximal concession, and capitulation on sovereignty-invading structural demands would be politically untenable. The action stance is a mild positive (negotiate): with the Xi-Trump meeting locked in for the G20, further escalation by us now would only invite the full $300B tariff round and deepen the export contraction; the wiser course is to press for a pause in escalation and a resumption of equal talks at Osaka, keeping our leverage in reserve rather than conceding upfront.

China May manufacturing PMI 49.4 (contraction), new-export orders 46.5, employment sub-index lowest since 2009
Yuan down ~3% since early May; IMF cut 2019 growth forecast to 6.2% (29-year low)
Threat of new US 25% tariffs on ~$300B of remaining exports
June 18 Trump-Xi phone call locks in G20 Osaka meeting — an opening for a pause and resumed talks
China's own leverage: rare-earth signal, unreliable-entity list threat, 'fight to the end' nationalist stance
